src/common/guard/jwt-two-factor.guard.ts: `JwtTwoFactorGuard extends AuthGuard('jwt-two-factor')` defines the same handleRequest body and the same pass-through canActivate
The two JWT guards differ only in the strategy name passed to AuthGuard(...), and the shared expired-token and unauthorized policy is copied rather than shared

parsedVerdict.reasoning: All four files are NestJS guards (throttling, JWT authentication, two-factor JWT authentication and route permission), so the module has one concern, request guarding. The rubric also fails a module that duplicates a rule which should live in one place, and this one does. JwtAuthGuard and JwtTwoFactorGuard contain the same `canActivate` and `handleRequest` bodies, character for character. That code is the policy for turning authentication failures into exceptions: an expired token becomes ForbiddenException('tokenExpired', StatusCodesList.TokenExpired), and an error or missing user is rethrown or becomes UnauthorizedException. Because it is copied, a change to it, such as a new status code or a refresh-token rule, has to be made in both files. The only real difference between the two classes is the passport strategy name, so the shared logic belongs in a base class or factory, for example a mixin that takes the strategy name. A smaller issue: PermissionGuard repeats its route-matching check (`route.path === path && route.method === method`) in both checkIfDefaultRoute and checkIfUserHavePermission. CustomThrottlerGuard is fine.

violations.message: JwtTwoFactorGuard.handleRequest and canActivate copy JwtAuthGuard: the TokenExpiredError -> ForbiddenException('tokenExpired', StatusCodesList.TokenExpired) mapping and the err/!user -> UnauthorizedException rule. This auth-failure policy should live in one shared base class or factory that takes the strategy name.
JwtAuthGuard.handleRequest holds the same token-expiry and unauthorized mapping that is copied in JwtTwoFactorGuard, so the invariant is defined in two places.
